analysis.one_liner: Extends enhanced ACA health insurance subsidies through 2029 and raises the income cap to qualify.
analysis.headline: Introduced November 10, 2025 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee; no committee action or vote has occurred, with the current enhanced subsidies set to lapse after 2025 under the bill's own text.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill keeps the enhanced Affordable Care Act premium tax credits — the subsidies that lower monthly health insurance premiums for people buying coverage on their own — from expiring, extending them through 2029. It also loosens who qualifies: today the subsidies cut off for households above 400% of the federal poverty level (roughly $62,000 for an individual), and this bill would raise that cap to 1,000%, letting far higher earners keep subsidized premiums. It would take effect starting in 2026.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy their own health insurance through the ACA marketplaces — including self-employed workers, small-business owners, early retirees, and families who don't get insurance through an employer. Without an extension, the enhanced subsidies expire after 2025 and monthly premiums for millions of enrollees would jump sharply; this bill keeps those lower premiums in place for four more years and extends subsidies to households earning well above the current cap.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the enhanced premium tax credit rules, currently set to run out before January 1, 2026, through the end of 2029 [S2].

Raises the income limit for receiving subsidies from 400% to 1,000% of the federal poverty level for years after 2025, so households far above the current cap can keep subsidized premiums instead of losing all assistance at once [S2].
Applies to tax years beginning after December 31, 2025, so it would kick in exactly when the current enhanced subsidies expire [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through higher federal spending on premium subsidies. The Congressional Budget Office estimates extensions of the enhanced credits cost tens of billions of dollars per year, though no cost estimate for this bill appears in the record. Raising the cap to 1,000% of poverty also directs a share of the added spending to upper-income households, not just low- and middle-income ones.

drawbacks.text: The bill raises the subsidy eligibility cap from 400% to 1,000% of the federal poverty level — roughly $150,000 for an individual and over $300,000 for a family of four — meaning a substantial share of the new federal spending would go to households far above middle income [S2].
The bill contains no offsetting revenue or spending cuts, so it adds directly to the federal deficit for five years [S2].

The subsidies flow through private insurers as premium payments, so much of the added federal spending becomes insurer revenue; critics argue that structure gives insurers little reason to restrain premiums.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly 20 million people enrolled in marketplace coverage, keeping the enhanced subsidies is the difference between affordable and sharply higher premiums, and the stakes are real. The costs are also real: the extension is unpaid-for federal spending, and the 1,000% income cap dilutes the program's focus by sending significant assistance up the income scale. A bill that simply extended the current 400% cap would be more targeted and cheaper; this version trades fiscal discipline for broader — and partly wealthier — eligibility.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Ways and Means Committee, which has taken no action on it, so it has gone nowhere while the subsidy expiration date arrives.

narrative.text: Rep. Brad Schneider introduced the bill on November 10, 2025, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which handles tax law [S1][S4].
Three Democratic colleagues cosponsored the bill; no Republicans appear among its supporters [S3].
The bill's own text shows the enhanced subsidy rules it would extend currently expire before January 1, 2026 [S2].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote on the bill appears in its action history [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has acted on the bill, so the practical winner so far is the status quo: the enhanced subsidies face expiration without this extension moving, which spares the federal budget new subsidy spending but leaves marketplace enrollees facing premium increases. Health insurers are indifferent so long as the question stays open.

for.name: Rep. Brad Schneider
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Keep Healthcare Affordable Act on November 10, 2025 to extend the enhanced ACA premium tax credits through 2029 and raise the income eligibility cap to 1,000% of poverty [S1][S2][S4].

for.name: Three Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsors, all Democrats [S3].

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on November 10, 2025 and has taken no action — no hearing, markup, or vote appears in the record [S4].

sides.party_line_note: Every listed supporter — the sponsor and all three cosponsors — is a Democrat, and no Republican support appears in the record [S3].

industries.industry: Health insurers selling ACA marketplace plans
industries.note: The bill keeps federal subsidy dollars flowing to insurers as premium payments through 2029 and expands the pool of subsidized customers by raising the income cap. Insurers collect the money while enrollees get the affordability relief; insurers' interest in continued subsidies runs alongside enrollees', though insurers also profit from the premium levels the subsidies absorb.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in Ways and Means with no Republican cosponsors and no committee action, in a chamber where the majority has not scheduled work on extending the enhanced credits through this vehicle. Standalone Democratic subsidy-extension bills introduced at this stage rarely reach the floor; the more likely path is that extension, if it happens at all, occurs through a broader negotiated package rather than this bill.
